rv.q: It's a brazenly straightforward drawing-room farce, created for light amusement and delivered on a platter by a properly silly cast of six.
Others will be ready to head to the basement bar at intermission to nurse their headache and remain there.
Over the course of an evening, the characters’ continual wink-and-nudge reminders of the goofiness of their world make it harder to maintain investment.

Given the year the play is set, these developments seem more a matter of pandering to contemporary ideas than anything else. But linear logic is not a hallmark of farce, good, bad or, as in this case, indifferent.
Tellingly, that physical prop gag is funnier than any one line of dialogue in this entire witless play.
The forbidden-fruit pleasures that “The Cottage” tries to pass off as a feast, in a lavish production directed by Jason Alexander, are familiar, superficial and fleeting.
Audience members seemed eager to yield to Rustin’s shticks and howl along, but in reality there’s more delight in looking at ‘The Cottage’ than laughing along to it.

...though ‘The Cottage’ operates like a farce it only rarely achieves a farce’s liftoff. That’s when the pressure on the characters becomes so intense that it initiates a kind of verbal and physical fission.
The Cottage is a fresh and fiercely fun play that's firing on all cylinders, with Rustin's excellent script.
Nonetheless, the cast consistently manages to make infidelity entertaining.
There are few things more pleasant on a steamy New York afternoon or evening than to sit down in a cool theater, turn off your brain, and laugh for two hours straight.
The Cottage is at its best when at its lightest.
The laughs are there, thanks to a comedically fine-tuned cast, but, befitting a bed-hopping plot, a tender, surprising altruism keeps them on your face.
That being said, I simply could not get into the play itself, which struck me as uninspired and utterly unfunny.
But the humor is so devoid of reality that the laughs become increasingly strained.
Sadly, it is not as funny as it thinks it is, or intends to be.

But long before the curtain call, not even the terrifically appealing cast nor the much-welcome air conditioning could dissuade me from seeing this ersatz 1920s British comedy of manners as a tedious two-hour exercise in comic overkill.

Sitting through this forced, unfunny take on British sex comedies of yore, I was reminded of an equally inept exercise in pandering to the tourist trade before that particular play was also run out of town.
This is farce with a capital “F.”
This is Jason Alexander‘s Broadway directorial debut and he shines in bringing all the varied pieces together to present a playdate of delight for everyone.

Even at its considerable best, the show is little more than a summertime distraction, but without its luxurious casting and ultra-polished design, “The Cottage” would seem like little more than a summer stock import or a decades-long-overdue transfer from the English stage.
This is a production that succeeds in its mission, solely to entertain and treat the audience to some lighthearted laughter.
“The Cottage” would have worked better as simply an outright farcical comedy with no attempt at seriousness.

For all the recent politicizing of the queer community’s lack of moral decency, The Cottage, which opens at Broadway’s Hayes Theater on July 24, is having a great time with extramarital merriment, heavy drinking, and more cigarette smoking than even the Marlboro Man could endure.
If not, don't waste your time and money.
Although the set sparkles, one expects the house itself will soon be vacant.

Although Sandy Rustin’s The Cottage, now arrived at Broadway’s Theater, bills itself as “A Romantic and (Not Quite) Murderous Comedy of Manners,” it is devoid of the two requirements of drawing room comedy: wit and quotable one-liners.
It's a tasteless, anything-goes enterprise that, ruthlessly milking its often-coarse comic bits, gives artifice a bad name.
